I'm a bit ignorant on this level of physics, as you can probably tell.

The resultant particle has to have integer charge. Individual quarks have the following charge states:

Charge 1st Gen 2nd Gen 3rd Gen
+2/3 up charm top
-1/3 down strange bottom

The antiquarks get the opposite charges:

Charge 1st Gen 2nd Gen 3rd Gen
-2/3 antiup anticharm antitop
+1/3 antidown antistrange antibottom

So you can combine them any way you like, provided the total charge is an integer. By far the most common (stable) states are mesons (quark+antiquark pair; can have charge -1, 0 or +1) and baryons (quark triplet; can have charge -2,-1,0,+1,+2).

Exotic things like the pentaquark were thought to be theoretically possible, but had never been observed before.

the Pentaquark was proposed as 4 quarks and an anti-quark so that the overall total was essentially 3?

It doesn't work that way.. you don't suddenly have 3 quarks if you have 4 and an antiquark. Anti is just a way for us to describe the same particle with inverted quantum numbers, but in nature it's just another particle - the "anti" doesn't mean it's some particle with negative mass that you can just subtract from others.

Now for quantum numbers asides from mass, it's possible there is some rule to what kind of combinations would be possible. Currently this rule is assumed to be that the charge of the particles need to add up to an integer value. However, to say that's inherent to the penta-quark itself rather than an emergent effect of this rule, is incorrect.

Just to add perspective... this is a nice discovery, but it's nowhere close in magnitude to the discovery of the Higgs boson a couple years back. The Higgs is an elementary particle, meaning it's not made up of smaller particles (although some theories suggest it may be composite). It was a fundamental piece of the electroweak force and explained why all known matter has mass. It was also the first scalar particle ever discovered.

The pentaquark is just a new arrangement of particles we already know about. The arrangement was predicted decades ago, and we've only now just reached a high enough energy level to produce it. It's cool to confirm that a pentaquark is possible, but it's nothing groundbreaking.

The next big discovery high-energy physicists at the LHC are looking for is the lightest supersymmetric particle, or maybe dark matter. Of course, many physicists don't think supersymmetry exists, but the gaping holes in the standard model, such as neutrino mass and the lack of gravity, lead most to believe there is something still out there to find.
